abstract: Background Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for health information and emotional support, yet little is known about their use for mental health by university students, a population with high digital literacy and elevated mental health need. Objective To estimate the prevalence of GenAI use for mental health support among respondents to a survey at a single UK university and to identify demographic and well-being characteristics associated with use. Methods Cross-sectional online survey of students at a large UK university. The primary outcome was self-reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. Well-being was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. Associations were examined using multivariable modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios. Results Of 22,207 students invited, 2020 responded (response rate 9.1%). Among respondents, 25.0% (n=503) reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. The most common reasons were advice when emotionally distressed (n=380, 19.3%), insights into mental health (n=256, 12.7%), and using GenAI as a personal therapist or coach (n=173, 8.6%); 2.7% (n=54) reported using GenAI to seek support when experiencing thoughts of self-harm. Use was more common among students aged 26-29 years, those identifying as Asian, students reporting a declared disability, students enrolled in management programs, and those with lower well-being. Conclusions Among respondents at a UK university, approximately one in four reported using GenAI for mental health support. Use was concentrated among students reporting poorer well-being and disability, suggesting that GenAI may function as an informal help-seeking pathway. Universities and health services should anticipate GenAI as a help-seeking pathway and ensure appropriate guidance, integration with existing services, and safeguards to support safe and equitable use.
